methodology: The study involved incorporating textile fibers from waste artificial leather into the structure of high-density fiberboards. The bulk density, modulus of elasticity, bending strength, screw withdrawal resistance, internal bond strength, and water absorption were measured for samples with varying content of recycled textile fibers.
research_objective: Establish the feasibility of incorporating textile fibers from waste artificial leather into the structure of high-density fiberboards to meet European standard requirements while mitigating environmental issues.

key_findings.finding: It is possible to meet the European standard requirements by adjusting technological parameters such as nominal density density.
The approach positively contributes to carbon capture and storage (CCS) policy and mitigates the problem of such waste being sent to landfills.
Incorporating recovered upholstery textile fibers as additives to wood fibers in HDF production is feasible, depending on the intended application of the HDF.

The use of textile waste in producing fiber boards can have a significant negative impact on mechanical properties such as internal bond strength and screw withdrawal resistance when increased content is used.
The textile fibers mixture contains 75% polyester and 25% of another material (likely referring to the aldehyde (UF) resin)
